tip_title: Your Home Policy Covers More Than Your House. But the Coverage on Everything Else Is Probably Lower Than You Think.
topic: Home Insurance - Other Structures Coverage Gap
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Home Policy Covers More Than Your House. But the Coverage on Everything Else Is Probably Lower Than You Think.**

Standard homeowners policies include what's called "other structures" coverage — that's your detached garage, fence, shed, or workshop sitting out back. The catch is that this coverage is typically set at 10% of your dwelling limit automatically. So if your home is insured for $450,000, you've got $45,000 spread across every outbuilding on the property. For a basic fence and a one-car garage, that might be fine. But if you've put real money into a workshop, a pool house, or a finished garage — that default number can leave a gap you won't notice until you're filing a claim. Pull up your declarations page and see what's sitting under "Coverage B."

Not sure if your other structures coverage reflects what you've actually got on the property? Your Peachy agent can take a look with you.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/how-much-homeowners-insurance-do-you-need)
summary: Covers the 'other structures' coverage (Coverage B) in standard homeowners policies — specifically that it defaults to 10% of the dwelling limit and may be inadequate for homeowners with detached garages, workshops, or outbuildings of meaningful value.
scoring_notes: East Cobb is 78% homeowners with $118k median HHI — exactly the audience that has detached garages, sheds, and finished outbuildings worth protecting. This is a coverage gap that hasn't been touched in the prior 6 months of tip history (all home tips covered dwelling limits, endorsements, water damage, sewer backup, roof maintenance, or personal property). The 10% default is a concrete, checkable number. Actionability is strong — reader can find 'Coverage B' on their declarations page today. Timeliness is evergreen (scored 6) but fits a fall renewal season when people are reviewing policies. Category diversifies from the flood tip above.

tip_title: FEMA Just Made It Easier to Buy Flood Insurance in Georgia. Here's the One Thing to Know.
topic: flood insurance Georgia NFIP - online purchase tool launch
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: FEMA Just Made It Easier to Buy Flood Insurance in Georgia. Here's the One Thing to Know.**

As of October 20, 2026, FEMA launched a new tool that lets Georgia residents buy a National Flood Insurance Program policy completely online through Floodsmart.gov. That's a real change — previously, the process ran through agents or write-your-own carriers, which added friction. The tool is available in any of the nearly 22,700 communities participating in the NFIP, and most Georgia ZIP codes qualify. The part most people still miss: there's a 30-day waiting period before a new NFIP flood policy kicks in. So if you've been putting this off, now is exactly the wrong time to keep waiting.

Not sure if you're in a flood zone or whether the NFIP is the right fit for your property? Your Peachy agent can walk through your options — takes about ten minutes.

📖 [Learn more from FEMA](https://www.fema.gov/press-release/20261020/fema-launches-new-option-buy-national-flood-insurance-program-policy-21)
summary: Covers FEMA's October 2026 launch of an online NFIP policy purchase tool available to Georgia residents via Floodsmart.gov, framed as a timely action item given the 30-day waiting period that makes procrastinating on flood coverage costly.
scoring_notes: Published October 20, 2026 — three days before this newsletter runs. Georgia-specific press release from FEMA makes this hyper-local and timely. Both newsletters have meaningful homeowner populations (East Cobb is 78%), and flood insurance is perennially underpurchased. Prior flood tips covered the building/contents election, ACV vs. replacement cost on contents, the 30-day waiting period urgency, and NFIP vs. private comparison — this tip is a new angle entirely: the just-launched direct online purchase tool as a concrete, action-now hook. The 30-day waiting period mention is a callback that reinforces prior education without repeating the same tip. High actionability because the reader can literally go to Floodsmart.gov today.

tip_title: Whole Life Insurance Has a 'Cash Value' Component. Here's What That Actually Means.
topic: Term Life vs. Whole Life Insurance - Cash Value Mechanics Explainer
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Whole Life Insurance Has a 'Cash Value' Component. Here's What That Actually Means.**

If you've ever seen a whole life policy and wondered what the cash value part actually does, here's the short version: a portion of your premium goes into an account that builds over time, and you can borrow against it or surrender the policy for that value if you ever stop paying. The tradeoff is that whole life costs significantly more than term life for the same death benefit amount. Term life covers you for a fixed window (10, 20, 30 years), has no cash value, and is generally the lower-cost option for people whose main goal is replacing income or covering debts if something happens to them. Neither is automatically better. The right one depends on what problem you're actually trying to solve.

Not sure which structure makes sense for where you are right now? Your Peachy agent can walk through the tradeoffs with you — no pressure, just clarity.

📖 [Learn more from NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/insurance/life/learn/term-vs-whole-life-insurance)
summary: Covers the cash value mechanics of whole life insurance specifically — what the cash value component is, how it builds, and how it compares functionally to term life — framed as a mechanics explainer rather than a which-should-I-buy decision framework.
scoring_notes: Repeat subject of term vs. whole life (prior tip: 2026-07-27), new angle: cash value mechanics explainer rather than which-type-fits-your-life-stage decision framework. All three audiences have median ages 36-42 with family and income profiles where whole-life cash-value confusion is common. October open enrollment adds a natural hook for life insurance conversations. NerdWallet is a trusted source. Selected under hard-minimum rule after all other candidate categories were eliminated — flood (over-covered, weak source content), home review (listicle sources), auto deductibles (non-trusted sources, over-covered). Best available option with a defensible fresh angle.
